screens.title: Implementing Private Data Collections in Chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how to keep sensitive data private inside a Hyperledger Fabric network while still proving its existence on the public ledger. We start by defining private data collections in a collection_config. json, a small file that declares which organizations may see raw private data, how long it lives, and how many peers should hold it. Next, you'll see the specific chaincode calls — PutPrivateData, GetPrivateData, and GetPrivateDataHash — and how to use GetTransient to pass private inputs securely from the client to chaincode without exposing them to ordering. You will also follow a concrete Go example that writes private details to a collection, stores the private-data hash publicly, and verifies hashes during later checks. Finally, we cover deployment: you must include --collections-config when committing the chaincode definition so all organizations agree on the collection. Why this matters: private collections let you meet compliance and confidentiality needs while preserving auditability. A common misconception is that private data never appears anywhere; in fact the hash is public to provide proof without revealing the raw payload. As you explore the lesson, look for where a client supplies transient data, where the chaincode stores raw bytes in the private store, and where it writes a hash to the public ledger. That mapping is the essential pattern to master.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Developer View
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll restate the objectives from the perspective of a developer building and deploying chaincode that uses private data collections. First, create a collection_config. json that names collections and encodes membership policies — this ensures only intended organizations store raw data and prevents accidental exposure. For example, an OR signature policy limits membership to listed MSPs. Second, implement chaincode functions to call PutPrivateData to persist raw bytes and GetPrivateData to read them on member peers; when non-members need assurance, use GetPrivateDataHash to retrieve the digest instead of raw content. Fourth, during lifecycle commit include --collections-config so every approver uses the same collection definitions. A common pitfall is a mismatch in collection name or forgetting the collections file during commit, both of which will break reads or writes. These developer skills combine code-level validation, correct A P I usage, and disciplined deployment.

screens.title: collection_config.json — structure and meaning
screens.narratorSegment: A private data collection is declared in a collection_config. json file that every approving organization agrees on. The essential fields are name, policy, requiredPeerCount, maxPeerCount, blockToLive, memberOnlyRead, and memberOnlyWrite. The name is the exact identifier you must reference in chaincode. The policy is a signature policy that controls which MSP members receive the raw private payload via gossip; a common form is OR('Org1MSP. member','Org2MSP. member'). RequiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount drive data availability: requiredPeerCount is a minimum number that should have the private data, ensuring it is retained across peers, while maxPeerCount limits how many peers will attempt to store it. blockToLive configures lifecycle: it is the number of blocks after which private data is purged on member peers — zero means keep forever, which has data-retention implications. Flags memberOnlyRead and memberOnlyWrite limit access so only members can read or write raw data. Finally, endorsementPolicy can optionally force certain endorsements for transactions that touch the collection. A frequent misconception is that the collection config is optional; in fact, failing to commit with a collections file means your chaincode cannot interact with PDCs. A concrete example is a JSON with name assetPrivateDetails, OR policy for Org1 and Org2, requiredPeerCount 1, maxPeerCount 2, and blockToLive 0 for indefinite retention. The takeaway: collection_config. json is the contract-level declaration of who can see, how long data lives, and how many peers will hold it. Always keep this file synchronized across approvals.

keyIdea.text: collection_config.json explicitly expresses membership, data retention, and availability; it must match across approvers and chaincode references.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › collection_config.json — structure
Definition

collection_config.json fields

name: Unique identifier referenced in chaincode APIs; must match exactly.
policy: Signature policy listing MSP members allowed to receive raw private data.
requiredPeerCount / maxPeerCount: Minimum and maximum peers that should receive private data for availability.
blockToLive: Number of blocks after which private data is purged (0 = infinite retention).
memberOnlyRead / memberOnlyWrite: Boolean flags restricting read/write to collection members.
Why it matters

The config enforces who gets raw data and how long it survives; mismatches or omissions break access and retention guarantees.

Example JSON
[
  {
    "name": "assetPrivateDetails",
    "policy": "OR('Org1MSP.member', 'Org2MSP.member')",
    "requiredPeerCount": 1,
    "maxPeerCount": 2,
    "blockToLive": 0,
    "memberOnlyRead": true,
    "memberOnlyWrite": true
  }
]
Common mistake
Collection name mismatch between config and chaincode prevents PutPrivateData/GetPrivateData from working.
Pro tip
Treat blockToLive carefully; set to 0 only when indefinite retention is acceptable for compliance.

screens.title: Chaincode APIs for private data
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric exposes a small set of chaincode APIs specifically for private data: PutPrivateData writes raw bytes into a named private collection; GetPrivateData retrieves raw bytes from that collection on peers that are members; GetPrivateDataHash returns the cryptographic hash of the private data record and is available to any peer on the channel. Understanding the access model is crucial: only peers that belong to the collection's policy will receive and persist the raw private data. A non-member peer calling GetPrivateData will receive nil or an error because it does not store raw content; however, that peer can call GetPrivateDataHash and obtain the digest recorded on the public ledger to verify integrity. PutPrivateData must use the same collection name as in collection_config. json — a simple string mismatch is a frequent runtime failure. PutPrivateData is used in conjunction with transient data: clients submit private payloads through the transient map, chaincode extracts the bytes and calls PutPrivateData with a key. When you need to prove a private payload without exposing it, store the hash in the public asset and retain the raw bytes only in the members' private stores. A practical example: a chaincode writes an asset's private price into assetPrivateDetails via PutPrivateData, then reads its hash and stores that hash in the public Asset record. Misconception to avoid: the hash is not secret — it is intentionally public so non-members can verify the supplied private data matches the ledger record. The takeaway: use Put/Get for raw content and GetPrivateDataHash for cross-organization verification.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Chaincode APIs for private data
Core Concept

PutPrivateData, GetPrivateData, GetPrivateDataHash

PutPrivateData(collection, key, value) — Persists raw bytes in the named private store accessible to collection members.
GetPrivateData(collection, key) — Returns raw bytes only if the peer hosts that collection.
GetPrivateDataHash(collection, key) — Returns the hash digest visible to all channel peers; used for verification by non-members.
Example
Write private price to assetPrivateDetails using PutPrivateData, then store the returned hash on the public asset record for verification.
Pitfall
A mismatched collection name yields silent failures; validate string constants carefully.
Quick Reference
Member peers: store raw data via PutPrivateData and serve GetPrivateData.
Non-member peers: use GetPrivateDataHash to verify without seeing raw payload.
Hashes are written to the public ledger so integrity checks are possible across organizations.
Key Takeaway

Use PutPrivateData/GetPrivateData for raw content and expose only the hash for cross-org verification.

screens.title: Handling transient data in chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: Transient data is the secure channel for private client inputs to chaincode proposals. Clients place sensitive payloads in the transient map when endorsing a transaction; these values are never serialized into the transaction proposal's payload and are not sent to the ordering service. Chaincode reads them with GetTransient, which returns a map of byte arrays keyed by string. Your chaincode must check that the expected key exists, unmarshal the JSON bytes, and validate required fields. The provided Go example uses transientMap, checks for asset_private_details, unmarshals into an AssetPrivateDetails struct, and errors out if the ID is missing. This validation is critical: missing keys or malformed JSON should cause the chaincode to return an error and fail endorsement, preventing an invalid private write. A common misconception is that transient data is stored anywhere on the ledger — it is not. However, if you mistakenly include transient data in the public write set, it will become visible. Keep transient bytes only inside the chaincode path that calls PutPrivateData to store the raw value in the private store. Concrete example: the Go chaincode retrieves transientMap := ctx. GetStub(). GetTransient(), extracts transientMap["asset_private_details"], unmarshals it, and then calls PutPrivateData on the collection. Remember also to compute the private data hash after PutPrivateData and store the hex-formatted hash in the public asset. The takeaway: treat transient data as ephemeral and validate it strictly before any private store operation.

keyIdea.title: Transient use
keyIdea.text: GetTransient provides ephemeral private inputs; validate and then use them to PutPrivateData so secrets never go to the ordering service.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Handling transient data
Code Walkthrough

GetTransient and validation

Follow these steps when handling transient data:
  1. Call ctx.GetStub().GetTransient() to obtain the transient map.
  2. Check for the expected key, for example "asset_private_details".
  3. Unmarshal the byte array into your private struct and validate required fields like ID.
  4. Call PutPrivateData with the collection name and key to persist raw bytes on member peers.
  5. Compute and store the private data hash on the public ledger for later verification.
Misconception
Transient data is not stored by the ordering service; however, mishandling it by writing it to public state will expose secrets.
Example excerpt (Go)
transientMap, err := ctx.GetStub().GetTransient()
if err != nil {
  return fmt.Errorf("error getting transient: %v", err)
}
privateDetailsJSON, ok := transientMap["asset_private_details"]
if !ok {
  return fmt.Errorf("asset_private_details key not found in transient data")
}
// unmarshal and validate ID before PutPrivateData
Key Takeaway

Always validate transient keys and JSON before writing private bytes to a collection to avoid silent failure or leakage.

screens.title: CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails — full Go flow
screens.narratorSegment: Let's trace a concrete Go function that implements the private-data pattern. The CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails function first calls GetTransient to retrieve the private JSON under the key asset_private_details. It unmarshals that JSON into an AssetPrivateDetails struct and validates that the ID field is present. Next it calls PutPrivateData with the collection name assetPrivateDetails and the ID as key; this writes the raw private JSON to the member peers' private stores via gossip. Immediately after, it calls GetPrivateDataHash for the same collection and key. The returned byte slice is a cryptographic hash of the private content. The chaincode then formats that hash as a hex string and includes it in a public Asset struct, which it marshals and writes to the public ledger via PutState. The pattern separates raw private storage from the public proof: raw bytes go only to member peers, while the hash stays on the channel ledger and serves as an immutable audit record. A typical error is to omit the hash step; without storing a public digest, non-member peers cannot verify a later provided private payload. Another pitfall is forgetting to call PutPrivateData before requesting the hash; ensure the private write succeeds before persisting or comparing its hash. The essential takeaway: the function maps transient input to a private store and publishes a hash that links private and public state securely.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails flow
Code Walkthrough

Transient to private store to public hash

// 1. Get transient data
transientMap, err := ctx.GetStub().GetTransient()
// 2. Extract asset_private_details and unmarshal
// 3. Put private data into collection
err = ctx.GetStub().PutPrivateData(collection, privateDetails.ID, privateDetailsJSON)
// 4. Get hash of private data
privateHash, err := ctx.GetStub().GetPrivateDataHash(collection, privateDetails.ID)
// 5. Create public asset with hash and PutState
Checkpoint
Always verify PutPrivateData succeeds before fetching the hash.
Why hash
The hash is public proof that links private content to ledger state without revealing secrets.
Scenario

A buyer and seller share private pricing via transient data. Members store the full price privately, while other organizations see only a hash stored in the public asset for audit.

Key Takeaway

Follow the sequence transient → PutPrivateData → GetPrivateDataHash → PutState to preserve privacy and traceability.

screens.title: Reading and verifying private data
screens.narratorSegment: Reading private details and verifying them against the public hash is a two-part operation with distinct access patterns. To read private details you call GetPrivateData with the collection name and key; this returns raw bytes only when the peer stores that collection. The provided Go function ReadPrivateAssetDetails calls GetPrivateData, checks for nil, unmarshals into the private struct, and returns it. For verification when a peer — possibly a non-member — needs to confirm that a provided private payload matches the public record, the chaincode uses GetTransient to accept a candidate private payload, computes its local hash, then reads the public asset via GetState to retrieve the stored hash. It compares the two hashes and returns true if they match. The example VerifyPrivateAssetDetails demonstrates this: it retrieves transient asset_private_details, computes hashOfProvidedPrivateData using ctx. GetStub(). GetHash(privateDetailsJSON), reads the public asset JSON, extracts asset. PrivateHash, and compares the hex-encoded values. Important distinctions: GetPrivateData returns raw content and requires membership; GetPrivateDataHash is universally readable and is the mechanism used to verify a private payload without revealing it. A typical error is trusting the presence of a public hash as proof that raw data currently exists on every member; blockToLive or deletion policies may have purged raw data even though the hash remains. The learning point: implement both read and verify functions carefully and check for missing data, parsing failures, and hash mismatches.

keyIdea.title: Read vs Verify
keyIdea.text: GetPrivateData returns raw bytes only for members; verification uses transient input, local hash computation, and comparison with the public hash stored in the asset record.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Reading and verifying private data
Definition

GetPrivateData and verification

Read: ctx.GetStub().GetPrivateData(collection, key) returns raw bytes for member peers; check for nil before unmarshalling.
Verify: Accept candidate private bytes via transient, compute hash locally, GetState to read stored public asset, compare stored hash with computed one.
Edge case
If blockToLive expired private data was purged, members may not find raw data even though the public hash remains; plan retention accordingly.
Example excerpt
hashOfProvidedPrivateData := ctx.GetStub().GetHash(privateDetailsJSON)
assetJSON, err := ctx.GetStub().GetState(assetID)
// unmarshal public asset and compare asset.PrivateHash to fmt.Sprintf("%x", hashOfProvidedPrivateData)
Key Takeaway

Use transient + local hash + public asset hash comparison to verify private payloads without revealing raw data to non-members.

screens.title: Deploying chaincode with private collections
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying chaincode that uses private data collections requires extra attention during the lifecycle commit. The key step is to include the collections file when approving and committing the chaincode definition so all organizations share the same collection metadata. The commands in the lesson illustrate packaging, installing, approving with --collections-config, and finally running peer lifecycle chaincode commitchanneldefinition with the --collections-config flag. In practice: package the chaincode, install it on each organization's peers, call approveformyorg for each organization and include the --collections-config path, and then call commitchanneldefinition with the same collections file and peer addresses. If any organization commits without the collections file or with a different version, chaincode interactions with PDCs will fail at runtime. Another common mistake is forgetting to pass the collections file path to the commit command; the chaincode will install but calls that reference collections will not behave as expected. screens.title: Public ledger vs Private Data Collections
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding whether data belongs on the public ledger or inside a private data collection is an architectural choice. Public ledger state is replicated to all peers and is suitable for information that must be visible to every organization, such as asset ownership or a public hash. Private Data Collections, by contrast, keep raw data only on member peers defined by the collection policy. Use PDCs for sensitive business details like price negotiations, personal identifiers, or contract terms that only a subset of participants should access. The typical pattern is to put minimal metadata or a hash on the public ledger while the confidential payload lives in a PDC. This gives both confidentiality and provable auditability. Some trade-offs: PDCs introduce complexity in lifecycle management — you must agree on the collection config and manage retention with blockToLive. Also, not all peers can run queries over private stores, so analytics across the whole network may be limited. A common misconception is that PDCs remove the need for strong peer security; in reality, private data is only as safe as the peers that host it — secure peer operations and access controls remain essential. A practical rule: store only what every org must see in public state; keep the rest in collections and expose only hashes publicly. This preserves confidentiality while enabling verification across the channel.

When to use each store

screens.title: Common mistakes and operational safety
screens.narratorSegment: Working with private data collections requires discipline to avoid common mistakes that lead to failures or unintentional exposure. First, collection name mismatch is a frequent runtime failure: the string used in PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData must exactly match the name in collection_config. json. Second, omitting --collections-config when committing the chaincode causes the chaincode to be unable to use PDCs on that channel; always include the file at approve and commit. Third, transient data handling errors — missing keys or failed JSON unmarshal — should be treated as hard errors that abort the transaction to avoid partial or inconsistent writes. Fourth, misconfigured blockToLive values can lead to premature deletion of private data; set it conservatively with compliance in mind. Fifth, do not assume that private data is safer than public state if peers are not secured; private data is only as secure as the peers that host it and their access controls. Finally, endorsement policies and optional endorsementPolicy fields for a collection can affect who must endorse transactions touching a collection; be sure these are aligned with your governance. A simple checklist prevents most issues: confirm exact names, include collections file at commit, validate transient payloads, set appropriate blockToLive, and secure private-data-holding peers. Following these safety practices will make PDC usage reliable in production.

Pitfalls and how to avoid them

Assuming private data never leaks is dangerous; secure peers and restrict access to private data stores.

screens.title: blockToLive and data lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: blockToLive controls how long private data remains in a peer's private data store before Fabric purges it. The value is expressed in blocks; setting blockToLive to zero means retain indefinitely. This setting has direct operational and compliance consequences. From a compliance perspective, indefinite retention may conflict with data deletion requests or regulations; from an availability perspective, too short a blockToLive can lead to private data being purged before peers that need it can access or reconstruct it, breaking verification or business processes. Design your blockToLive around expected data access patterns, archival requirements, and legal obligations. If you require long-term proof but short-term raw access, one approach is to store the hash on the public ledger (which remains indefinitely) and keep raw data in the PDC for a limited time. That way you can later verify a private payload against the permanent public hash even after raw data removals. Operationally, purging reduces storage demands on private stores but increases the need for active archival strategies. In short, choose blockToLive deliberately: it is a retention control that bridges privacy, compliance, and operational cost.

Definition

blockToLive explained

blockToLive specifies how many blocks after commitment private data persists in member peers' private stores. A value of 0 means the data is kept forever.

Short blockToLive reduces storage but risks losing data needed later.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to keep sensitive data private inside a Hyperledger Fabric network while still proving its existence on the public ledger. We start by defining private data collections in a collection_config. json, a small file that declares which organizations may see raw private data, how long it lives, and how many peers should hold it. Next, you'll see the specific chaincode calls — PutPrivateData, GetPrivateData, and GetPrivateDataHash — and how to use GetTransient to pass private inputs securely from the client to chaincode without exposing them to ordering. You will also follow a concrete Go example that writes private details to a collection, stores the private-data hash publicly, and verifies hashes during later checks. Finally, we cover deployment: you must include --collections-config when committing the chaincode definition so all organizations agree on the collection. Why this matters: private collections let you meet compliance and confidentiality needs while preserving auditability. A common misconception is that private data never appears anywhere; in fact the hash is public to provide proof without revealing the raw payload. As you explore the lesson, look for where a client supplies transient data, where the chaincode stores raw bytes in the private store, and where it writes a hash to the public ledger. That mapping is the essential pattern to master.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define a private data collection configuration, implement chaincode calls to store and retrieve private data, handle transient inputs safely, and deploy chaincode that includes the private collection definition. First, defining a collection involves writing a collection_config. json with fields such as name, policy, requiredPeerCount, maxPeerCount, blockToLive, and memberOnlyRead/memberOnlyWrite. That matters because a mismatch or omission can break access or data retention. Second, you'll write chaincode that uses PutPrivateData to write raw private bytes, GetPrivateData to retrieve those bytes on member peers, and GetPrivateDataHash to publish a verifiable digest on the public ledger. Third, you will use GetTransient to accept private inputs from the client that never transit the ordering service. Lastly, you will package and commit chaincode with the --collections-config flag so all organizations agree on the collection. A typical example is storing sensitive asset pricing details privately while storing only a hash in the public asset record. Keep in mind that these are practical developer skills: validation of transient data, exact collection name matching, and agreeing on blockToLive are common operational checks you must perform.

Now we'll restate the objectives from the perspective of a developer building and deploying chaincode that uses private data collections. First, create a collection_config. json that names collections and encodes membership policies — this ensures only intended organizations store raw data and prevents accidental exposure. For example, an OR signature policy limits membership to listed MSPs. Second, implement chaincode functions to call PutPrivateData to persist raw bytes and GetPrivateData to read them on member peers; when non-members need assurance, use GetPrivateDataHash to retrieve the digest instead of raw content. Third, accept private inputs through GetTransient so client secrets are never sent to the ordering service. Validate presence and format; missing keys cause failures. Fourth, during lifecycle commit include --collections-config so every approver uses the same collection definitions. A common pitfall is a mismatch in collection name or forgetting the collections file during commit, both of which will break reads or writes. These developer skills combine code-level validation, correct A P I usage, and disciplined deployment.

A private data collection is declared in a collection_config. json file that every approving organization agrees on. The essential fields are name, policy, requiredPeerCount, maxPeerCount, blockToLive, memberOnlyRead, and memberOnlyWrite. The name is the exact identifier you must reference in chaincode. The policy is a signature policy that controls which MSP members receive the raw private payload via gossip; a common form is OR('Org1MSP. member','Org2MSP. member'). RequiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount drive data availability: requiredPeerCount is a minimum number that should have the private data, ensuring it is retained across peers, while maxPeerCount limits how many peers will attempt to store it. blockToLive configures lifecycle: it is the number of blocks after which private data is purged on member peers — zero means keep forever, which has data-retention implications. Flags memberOnlyRead and memberOnlyWrite limit access so only members can read or write raw data. Finally, endorsementPolicy can optionally force certain endorsements for transactions that touch the collection. A frequent misconception is that the collection config is optional; in fact, failing to commit with a collections file means your chaincode cannot interact with PDCs. A concrete example is a JSON with name assetPrivateDetails, OR policy for Org1 and Org2, requiredPeerCount 1, maxPeerCount 2, and blockToLive 0 for indefinite retention. The takeaway: collection_config. json is the contract-level declaration of who can see, how long data lives, and how many peers will hold it. Always keep this file synchronized across approvals.

Fabric exposes a small set of chaincode APIs specifically for private data: PutPrivateData writes raw bytes into a named private collection; GetPrivateData retrieves raw bytes from that collection on peers that are members; GetPrivateDataHash returns the cryptographic hash of the private data record and is available to any peer on the channel. Understanding the access model is crucial: only peers that belong to the collection's policy will receive and persist the raw private data. A non-member peer calling GetPrivateData will receive nil or an error because it does not store raw content; however, that peer can call GetPrivateDataHash and obtain the digest recorded on the public ledger to verify integrity. PutPrivateData must use the same collection name as in collection_config. json — a simple string mismatch is a frequent runtime failure. PutPrivateData is used in conjunction with transient data: clients submit private payloads through the transient map, chaincode extracts the bytes and calls PutPrivateData with a key. When you need to prove a private payload without exposing it, store the hash in the public asset and retain the raw bytes only in the members' private stores. A practical example: a chaincode writes an asset's private price into assetPrivateDetails via PutPrivateData, then reads its hash and stores that hash in the public Asset record. Misconception to avoid: the hash is not secret — it is intentionally public so non-members can verify the supplied private data matches the ledger record. The takeaway: use Put/Get for raw content and GetPrivateDataHash for cross-organization verification.

Transient data is the secure channel for private client inputs to chaincode proposals. Clients place sensitive payloads in the transient map when endorsing a transaction; these values are never serialized into the transaction proposal's payload and are not sent to the ordering service. Chaincode reads them with GetTransient, which returns a map of byte arrays keyed by string. Your chaincode must check that the expected key exists, unmarshal the JSON bytes, and validate required fields. The provided Go example uses transientMap, checks for asset_private_details, unmarshals into an AssetPrivateDetails struct, and errors out if the ID is missing. This validation is critical: missing keys or malformed JSON should cause the chaincode to return an error and fail endorsement, preventing an invalid private write. A common misconception is that transient data is stored anywhere on the ledger — it is not. However, if you mistakenly include transient data in the public write set, it will become visible. Keep transient bytes only inside the chaincode path that calls PutPrivateData to store the raw value in the private store. Concrete example: the Go chaincode retrieves transientMap := ctx. GetStub(). GetTransient(), extracts transientMap["asset_private_details"], unmarshals it, and then calls PutPrivateData on the collection. Remember also to compute the private data hash after PutPrivateData and store the hex-formatted hash in the public asset. The takeaway: treat transient data as ephemeral and validate it strictly before any private store operation.

Let's trace a concrete Go function that implements the private-data pattern. The CreateAssetWithPrivateDetails function first calls GetTransient to retrieve the private JSON under the key asset_private_details. It unmarshals that JSON into an AssetPrivateDetails struct and validates that the ID field is present. Next it calls PutPrivateData with the collection name assetPrivateDetails and the ID as key; this writes the raw private JSON to the member peers' private stores via gossip. Immediately after, it calls GetPrivateDataHash for the same collection and key. The returned byte slice is a cryptographic hash of the private content. The chaincode then formats that hash as a hex string and includes it in a public Asset struct, which it marshals and writes to the public ledger via PutState. The pattern separates raw private storage from the public proof: raw bytes go only to member peers, while the hash stays on the channel ledger and serves as an immutable audit record. A typical error is to omit the hash step; without storing a public digest, non-member peers cannot verify a later provided private payload. Another pitfall is forgetting to call PutPrivateData before requesting the hash; ensure the private write succeeds before persisting or comparing its hash. The essential takeaway: the function maps transient input to a private store and publishes a hash that links private and public state securely.

Reading private details and verifying them against the public hash is a two-part operation with distinct access patterns. To read private details you call GetPrivateData with the collection name and key; this returns raw bytes only when the peer stores that collection. The provided Go function ReadPrivateAssetDetails calls GetPrivateData, checks for nil, unmarshals into the private struct, and returns it. For verification when a peer — possibly a non-member — needs to confirm that a provided private payload matches the public record, the chaincode uses GetTransient to accept a candidate private payload, computes its local hash, then reads the public asset via GetState to retrieve the stored hash. It compares the two hashes and returns true if they match. The example VerifyPrivateAssetDetails demonstrates this: it retrieves transient asset_private_details, computes hashOfProvidedPrivateData using ctx. GetStub(). GetHash(privateDetailsJSON), reads the public asset JSON, extracts asset. PrivateHash, and compares the hex-encoded values. Important distinctions: GetPrivateData returns raw content and requires membership; GetPrivateDataHash is universally readable and is the mechanism used to verify a private payload without revealing it. A typical error is trusting the presence of a public hash as proof that raw data currently exists on every member; blockToLive or deletion policies may have purged raw data even though the hash remains. The learning point: implement both read and verify functions carefully and check for missing data, parsing failures, and hash mismatches.

Deploying chaincode that uses private data collections requires extra attention during the lifecycle commit. The key step is to include the collections file when approving and committing the chaincode definition so all organizations share the same collection metadata. The commands in the lesson illustrate packaging, installing, approving with --collections-config, and finally running peer lifecycle chaincode commitchanneldefinition with the --collections-config flag. In practice: package the chaincode, install it on each organization's peers, call approveformyorg for each organization and include the --collections-config path, and then call commitchanneldefinition with the same collections file and peer addresses. If any organization commits without the collections file or with a different version, chaincode interactions with PDCs will fail at runtime. Another common mistake is forgetting to pass the collections file path to the commit command; the chaincode will install but calls that reference collections will not behave as expected. The activity section gives a full set of terminal steps for packaging, installing, approving, committing, and invoking InitLedger with isInit. Keep certificate file paths and peer TLS roots accurate when running these commands. The practical takeaway: the collections file is part of the chaincode definition consensus — include it at approval and commit or the privacy guarantees won't hold.

Deciding whether data belongs on the public ledger or inside a private data collection is an architectural choice. Public ledger state is replicated to all peers and is suitable for information that must be visible to every organization, such as asset ownership or a public hash. Private Data Collections, by contrast, keep raw data only on member peers defined by the collection policy. Use PDCs for sensitive business details like price negotiations, personal identifiers, or contract terms that only a subset of participants should access. The typical pattern is to put minimal metadata or a hash on the public ledger while the confidential payload lives in a PDC. This gives both confidentiality and provable auditability. Some trade-offs: PDCs introduce complexity in lifecycle management — you must agree on the collection config and manage retention with blockToLive. Also, not all peers can run queries over private stores, so analytics across the whole network may be limited. A common misconception is that PDCs remove the need for strong peer security; in reality, private data is only as safe as the peers that host it — secure peer operations and access controls remain essential. A practical rule: store only what every org must see in public state; keep the rest in collections and expose only hashes publicly. This preserves confidentiality while enabling verification across the channel.

Next, package the chaincode using peer lifecycle chaincode package. Install the package on each organization's peers and capture the package IDs. This activity is practical: it exercises packaging, approval with collections, and end-to-end validation of private data handling.

Working with private data collections requires discipline to avoid common mistakes that lead to failures or unintentional exposure. First, collection name mismatch is a frequent runtime failure: the string used in PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData must exactly match the name in collection_config. json. Second, omitting --collections-config when committing the chaincode causes the chaincode to be unable to use PDCs on that channel; always include the file at approve and commit. Third, transient data handling errors — missing keys or failed JSON unmarshal — should be treated as hard errors that abort the transaction to avoid partial or inconsistent writes. Fourth, misconfigured blockToLive values can lead to premature deletion of private data; set it conservatively with compliance in mind. Fifth, do not assume that private data is safer than public state if peers are not secured; private data is only as secure as the peers that host it and their access controls. Finally, endorsement policies and optional endorsementPolicy fields for a collection can affect who must endorse transactions touching a collection; be sure these are aligned with your governance. A simple checklist prevents most issues: confirm exact names, include collections file at commit, validate transient payloads, set appropriate blockToLive, and secure private-data-holding peers. Following these safety practices will make PDC usage reliable in production.

blockToLive controls how long private data remains in a peer's private data store before Fabric purges it. The value is expressed in blocks; setting blockToLive to zero means retain indefinitely. This setting has direct operational and compliance consequences. From a compliance perspective, indefinite retention may conflict with data deletion requests or regulations; from an availability perspective, too short a blockToLive can lead to private data being purged before peers that need it can access or reconstruct it, breaking verification or business processes. Design your blockToLive around expected data access patterns, archival requirements, and legal obligations. If you require long-term proof but short-term raw access, one approach is to store the hash on the public ledger (which remains indefinitely) and keep raw data in the PDC for a limited time. That way you can later verify a private payload against the permanent public hash even after raw data removals. Operationally, purging reduces storage demands on private stores but increases the need for active archival strategies. In short, choose blockToLive deliberately: it is a retention control that bridges privacy, compliance, and operational cost.

Let's summarize the most important concepts to remember. First, collection_config. json defines the identity, membership policy, requiredPeerCount and blockToLive for private data collections; keep it consistent across approvers. Second, PutPrivateData writes raw private bytes to a named collection and GetPrivateData reads those bytes only on member peers. Third, GetPrivateDataHash returns a digest usable by any peer to verify a supplied private payload without exposing the raw content. Hold these ideas in mind as the core mechanics for private data in Fabric: declaration via the collection config, private writes on member peers, and public hashes for verification. These three items are the building blocks for secure, auditable private data patterns in chaincode.
